A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, research questions, core theory, algorithm and retained experiments. All 25 pages of v1 and 30 pages of v2, including appendices and visual material, support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original MARL experiments in discrete and continuous matrix games and Multi-Goal-Capture, including observability tests and HED parameter-search results.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds tag, football, larger-team matrix-game and adverse-initialization experiments.

M1.justification: HED is renamed HetGPS, but Algorithm 1 retains the same rollouts, heterogeneity-gain objective, environment-gradient update and policy-training steps. The policy architecture also remains unchanged. Appendix P expands discussion of possible non-differentiable variants without specifying a substantive new algorithm.

E1.justification: v2 adds two materially different evaluated tasks: 2v2 tag with moving heuristic escapees, obstacles and sparse capture rewards, and a football drill requiring scoring and opponent blocking under a composite reward. Matrix games and Multi-Goal-Capture remain. Colonel Blotto and level-based foraging remain analytical examples.

E2.justification: The experimental comparison remains MAPPO with shared versus independent agent parameters. The added environments reuse this comparison and existing aggregator choices. PAIRED, Designer-RL and evolutionary approaches are discussed, but no experimental comparison against another environment-search algorithm is added.

E3.justification: New protocols include football training for 500 iterations of 240,000 frames with opponent speed annealed from 0% to 100%, and tag training for 30 million frames. Appendix J adds an eight-agent/eight-task matrix configuration; Appendix Q adds adverse Softmax initialization and measurements through 100 million frames. These supplement the retained protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds scalability analysis at N=M=8, an initialization-robustness test starting with unfavorable aggregator temperatures, and football controls testing whether heterogeneity benefits depend on reward structure. Figures 8–9 add behavioral case studies. The original observability analysis is retained and relocated, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v2 adds explicit replication counts for the new studies: eight seeds for the larger matrix game, six for football and three for adverse initialization. Retained experiments keep their previous seed counts and mean/standard-deviation reporting. This documents additional replication designs, not increased runs for the original experiments or new significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: Tables 5–8 retain their numerical values. New results include tag gains in Figure 4b, larger-team gains in Table 9, and football gains of 1.76±0.72 for (U=min,T=max) and 1.18±0.11 for (U=mean,T=max), alongside near-zero control means in Table 10. Table 11 reports recovery from adverse initialization. These are results under added settings, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: Theorems 3.1–3.4, their proofs and the existing aggregator derivations are retained. v2 removes v1's explicit conjecture that the Softmax lower bound is exact and removes 'Exact' from Theorem 3.4's title. Appendix P.1 explicitly formulates the optimized-policy Stackelberg objective, without adding a convergence theorem or proof.

C1.justification: Both versions make the same central contributions: curvature-based characterization of heterogeneity gains and gradient-based environment-parameter search for favorable reward regimes. v2 clarifies the behavioral meaning of heterogeneity and provides broader experimental support, but does not substantively replace or redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: v2 interprets football results as evidence of applicability when double aggregation forms only part of the reward, explains Softmax parameter variance through saturation, and expands discussion of convergence and non-differentiable alternatives. It also sharpens the neural-versus-behavioral distinction. Conversely, v1's explicit limitation concerning inseparable tasks disappears without a corresponding extension of the theory.

D1.justification: v2 adds a supplementary website and visualization links, documents the new task reward constructions and training settings, and reports single-L40 iteration timings of approximately 15 seconds without environment backpropagation versus 20 seconds with it. MAPPO, VMAS/TorchRL, two-layer 256-unit Tanh networks and the supplementary code/YAML disclosure remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds Amir et al. on RECODE, Simaan and Cruz on Stackelberg games, and Stanley et al. on neuroevolution, supporting expanded co-design and optimization discussion. The main diversity literature and relationship to PAIRED remain. The System Neural Diversity preprint-to-journal update concerns the same cited work.

P1.justification: v2 renames HED to HetGPS, refines terminology and introductory explanations, and condenses the experimental narrative by moving Multi-Goal-Capture details and observability discussion into appendices. The principal section sequence and most theoretical and algorithmic exposition remain intact; this is a targeted reorganization rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adopts the ICLR layout, revises curve styling and legends, adds the tag panel, Figures 8–9 and Tables 9–11, and relocates the original observability panel to Figure 10. These substantially change the visual presentation. New problems include incorrect duplicate legend entries in Figures 3 and 4a and an extra Figure 11 caption attached to the observability plot.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical bridge between the theory and embodied learning. Tag tests sparse discrete rewards; football tests a composite reward with controls; and Appendix Q addresses whether search succeeds from unfavorable initialization. These resolve important gaps in v1's narrower validation, while clearer behavioral-versus-neural distinctions improve interpretation. The legend/caption errors and removed inseparability caveat are drawbacks, but do not outweigh the added targeted evidence.
